To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the long-term sea level trend is not uniform around the global oceans; its regional patterns are closely related to the climate system; the ENSO and the PDO are important factors that can be used to describe the long-term regional trend in mean sea level.

the long-term regional trend of mean sea level can be better estimated by multiple regression than by simple linear regression, and that the Pacific Decadal oscillation (PDO) has a stronger impact on mean sea level than El Niño–southern oscillation (ENSO) in the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
the regional patterns associated with climatological factors vary greatly in different basines, notably in the Eastern and Western regions of the Pacific ocean.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long-term regional mean sea level change in the global oceans and the impact of climatic factors, especially the ENSO and PDO, on the regional sea level change.
the long-term regional trend of mean sea level and the impact of climate factors on it.
the long-term regional trend in mean sea level and its variability over 22 years, from the beginning of the satellite altimetric era to the present.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the regional sea level trend and its variability are not only controlled by global warming but are also influenced by the climate system.
regional patterns of mean sea level change are not uniform, and the long-term spatial variability and trends are closely associated with prevailing climate factors.

the regional mean sea level change is the result of the superimposition of various climatic factors, including the ENSO, PDO, and the Indian Ocean Dipole, which are all closely related to the fluctuations in the climate system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ENSO is a dominant factor in the tropical Pacific, while the PDO is a dominant factor over the mid-latitudes.
the long-term regional mean sea level trend can be well explained by the ENSO and the PDO.
the long-term regional trend in sea level change during the altimetric era was dominated by a warming climate and the associated sea level rise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the long-term regional mean sea level is not only a function of the global sea level rise, but it is also influenced by the regional climate variability.
regional mean sea level changes are not uniform, and that the ENSO and the PDO are the most important climate signals in explaining the regional mean sea level variations.
regional patterns of long-term sea level change are closely associated with climatic variability, which should be taken into account in future sea level rise projections.
